claim: Cryptococcal meningitis has high mortality.
source: Background:Cryptococcal meningitis has high mortality.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract background section, drawing from established scientific knowledge about cryptococcal meningitis outcomes.

claim: Flucytosine is a key treatment for cryptococcal meningitis but is expensive and rarely available.
source: Flucytosine is a key treatment but is expensive and rarely available.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about flucytosine's role and accessibility issues in treating cryptococcal meningitis.

claim: Tamoxifen has synergistic anti-cryptococcal activity with amphotericin in vitro.
source: The anticancer agent tamoxifen has synergistic anti-cryptococcal activity with amphotericin in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research and is referenced as established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Tamoxifen is off-patent, cheap, and widely available.
source: It is off-patent, cheap, and widely available.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the commercial and availability status of tamoxifen, based on general pharmaceutical knowledge.

claim: Fifty patients were enrolled in the trial with a median age of 34 years and 35 males.
source: Fifty patients were enrolled (median age 34 years, 35 male).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the trial enrollment data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tamoxifen had no effect on Early Fungicidal Activity (EFA).
source: Tamoxifen had no effect on EFA (−0.48log10 colony-forming units/mL/CSF control arm versus −0.49 tamoxifen arm, difference −0.005log10CFU/ml/day, 95% CI: −0.16, 0.15, p=0.95).
evidence: This claim is supported by the primary outcome data from the trial showing no significant difference between treatment arms.

claim: Tamoxifen caused QTc prolongation.
source: Tamoxifen caused QTc prolongation.
evidence: This claim is supported by adverse event data collected during the trial.

claim: High-dose tamoxifen does not increase the clearance rate of Cryptococcus from CSF.
source: Conclusions:High-dose tamoxifen does not increase the clearance rate of Cryptococcus from CSF.
evidence: This conclusion is directly supported by the primary outcome data from the trial.

claim: There were an estimated 223,000 cases of cryptococcal meningitis in 2014.
source: Cryptococcal meningitis is a leading cause of death in HIV-infected patients, with an estimated 223,000 cases in 2014 (Rajasingham et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rajasingham et al., 2017.

claim: The vast majority of cryptococcal meningitis infections are due to C. neoformans and occur in low-income tropical settings.
source: The vast majority of infections are due to C. neoformans, and occur in low-income tropical settings.
evidence: This statement reflects established epidemiological knowledge about cryptococcal meningitis.

claim: Current international guidelines recommend initial induction treatment with amphotericin combined with flucytosine, followed by consolidation therapy with fluconazole.
source: Current international guidelines recommend initial induction treatment with amphotericin combined with flucytosine, followed by consolidation therapy with fluconazole (World Health Organization, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to WHO 2018 guidelines.

claim: The combination of amphotericin and flucytosine delivers the fastest rates of clearance of yeast from cerebrospinal fluid and the best survival rates.
source: This combination delivers the fastest rates of clearance of yeast from cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and the best survival rates (Day et al., 2013; Molloy et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Day et al., 2013 and Molloy et al., 2018.

claim: Even on gold standard therapy, 30% of patients will die within 10 weeks of diagnosis.
source: However, even on this gold standard therapy, 30% of patients will die within 10 weeks of diagnosis (Day et al., 2013; Molloy et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Day et al., 2013 and Molloy et al., 2018.

claim: Adjunctive therapy with corticosteroids results in worse outcomes in cryptococcal meningitis.
source: Adjunctive therapy with corticosteroids, which has proven beneficial in other forms of meningitis, results in worse outcomes (Beardsley et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Beardsley et al., 2016.

claim: Cryptococcal meningitis can occur in HIV-uninfected patients, including immunocompetent people and those with other causes of immunosuppression.
source: Cryptococcal meningitis can also occur in HIV-uninfected patients, including immunocompetent people and those with other causes of immunosuppression.
evidence: This statement reflects established clinical knowledge about cryptococcal meningitis epidemiology.

claim: Survival rates in HIV-uninfected patients with cryptococcal meningitis are similar to those seen in HIV-infected patients.
source: Survival rates are similar to those seen in HIV-infected patients.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge about outcomes in different patient populations.

claim: In Vietnam around 20% of cases of cryptococcal meningitis are in HIV-uninfected patients.
source: In Vietnam around 20% of cases of cryptococcal meningitis are in HIV-uninfected patients (Chau et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chau et al., 2010.

claim: Disease in Vietnam is predominantly due to the C. neoformans VNIa-5 lineage.
source: Disease is predominantly due to the C. neoformans VNIa-5 lineage; C. gattii is responsible for around 25% of cases (Chau et al., 2010; Ashton et al., 2019; Day et al., 2011; Day et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Chau et al., 2010; Ashton et al., 2019; Day et al., 2011; Day et al., 2017).

claim: C. gattii is responsible for around 25% of cryptococcal meningitis cases in Vietnam.
source: Disease is predominantly due to the C. neoformans VNIa-5 lineage; C. gattii is responsible for around 25% of cases (Chau et al., 2010; Ashton et al., 2019; Day et al., 2011; Day et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Amphotericin and flucytosine are each more than 60 years old.
source: Amphotericin and flucytosine are each more than 60 years old; the last novel drug class developed was the azoles, introduced 30 years ago.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the age of these antifungal drugs, based on pharmaceutical history knowledge.

claim: The last novel antifungal drug class developed was the azoles, introduced 30 years ago.
source: Amphotericin and flucytosine are each more than 60 years old; the last novel drug class developed was the azoles, introduced 30 years ago.
evidence: This is a factual statement about pharmaceutical development history.

claim: Access to flucytosine is severely restricted by availability and cost.
source: Access to flucytosine is severely restricted by availability and cost, meaning it is rarely used where disease burden is highest.
evidence: This statement reflects known issues with flucytosine access in resource-limited settings.

claim: A 2-week course of flucytosine now costs around 30,000 USD in the USA.
source: Despite being off-patent, it has been subject to extraordinary price rises in recent years, with a 2-week course now costs around 30,000 USD in the USA (Merry and Boulware, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Merry and Boulware, 2016.

claim: Tamoxifen has anti-cryptococcal activity and appears to act synergistically when combined with other antifungals against the type strain in vitro.
source: Tamoxifen, a selective estrogen receptor modulator used to treat breast cancer, has anti-cryptococcal activity, appearing to act synergistically when combined with other antifungals against the type strain in vitro, and to be fungicidal when combined with fluconazole in the mouse infection model (Butts et al., 2014; Dolan et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Butts et al., 2014 and Dolan et al., 2009.

claim: Tamoxifen is fungicidal when combined with fluconazole in the mouse infection model.
source: Tamoxifen, a selective estrogen receptor modulator used to treat breast cancer, has anti-cryptococcal activity, appearing to act synergistically when combined with other antifungals against the type strain in vitro, and to be fungicidal when combined with fluconazole in the mouse infection model (Butts et al., 2014; Dolan et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Butts et al., 2014 and Dolan et al., 2009.

claim: Tamoxifen acts synergistically with amphotericin against two-thirds of clinical isolates of Cryptococcus neoformans and C. gattii from the study archive.
source: We found it to act synergistically with amphotericin against two-thirds of clinical isolates of Cryptococcus neoformans and C. gattii from our archive and to have an additive interaction when combined with fluconazole in vitro (Hai et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hai et al., 2019, which reports the authors' own previous research.

claim: Tamoxifen has an additive interaction when combined with fluconazole in vitro.
source: We found it to act synergistically with amphotericin against two-thirds of clinical isolates of Cryptococcus neoformans and C. gattii from our archive and to have an additive interaction when combined with fluconazole in vitro (Hai et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hai et al., 2019.

claim: Tamoxifen is concentrated in brain tissue 10- to 100-fold compared with plasma.
source: Tamoxifen is concentrated in brain tissue (10- to 100-fold compared with plasma) and macrophage phagosomes (a site of growth for Cryptococcus spp.), is off-patent, cheap (~10US cents/tablet) and widely available (Lien et al., 1991a; Lien et al., 1991b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lien et al., 1991a and Lien et al., 1991b.

claim: Tamoxifen is concentrated in macrophage phagosomes, a site of growth for Cryptococcus spp.
source: Tamoxifen is concentrated in brain tissue (10- to 100-fold compared with plasma) and macrophage phagosomes (a site of growth for Cryptococcus spp.), is off-patent, cheap (~10US cents/tablet) and widely available (Lien et al., 1991a; Lien et al., 1991b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lien et al., 1991a and Lien et al., 1991b.

claim: Tamoxifen costs approximately 10 US cents per tablet.
source: Tamoxifen is concentrated in brain tissue (10- to 100-fold compared with plasma) and macrophage phagosomes (a site of growth for Cryptococcus spp.), is off-patent, cheap (~10US cents/tablet) and widely available (Lien et al., 1991a; Lien et al., 1991b).
evidence: This is a factual statement about tamoxifen pricing.

claim: Doses 5- to 10-fold that used in breast cancer should deliver plasma concentrations of tamoxifen greater than the MIC90 of Vietnamese clinical isolates.
source: Pharmacokinetic data suggest that doses 5- to 10-fold that used in breast cancer (typically 30 mg/day) should deliver plasma concentrations of tamoxifen greater than the Minimum Inhibitory Concentration 90 (MIC90 16 µg/mL) of Vietnamese clinical isolates (Lien et al., 1991a).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from pharmacokinetic data cited from Lien et al., 1991a.

claim: High doses of tamoxifen (5- to 10-fold that used in breast cancer) have been used and well-tolerated in small cell lung cancer, desmoid tumours, and prostate cancer.
source: Such doses have been used, and well-tolerated, in small cell lung cancer, desmoid tumours, and prostate cancer.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge from prior clinical use of high-dose tamoxifen in other conditions.

claim: Acute side effects of tamoxifen that could be detrimental from short-course treatment include QT prolongation of the cardiac de/repolarization cycle.
source: While generally well-tolerated, acute side effects that could be detrimental from short-course treatment include QT prolongation of the cardiac de/repolarization cycle, although the risk of life-threatening arrhythmias appears to be low (Grouthier et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Grouthier et al., 2018.

claim: The risk of life-threatening arrhythmias from tamoxifen appears to be low.
source: While generally well-tolerated, acute side effects that could be detrimental from short-course treatment include QT prolongation of the cardiac de/repolarization cycle, although the risk of life-threatening arrhythmias appears to be low (Grouthier et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Grouthier et al., 2018.

claim: In Vietnam, induction treatment for cryptococcal meningitis consists of amphotericin combined with fluconazole.
source: In Vietnam induction treatment for cryptococcal meningitis consists of amphotericin combined with fluconazole, consistent with WHO recommendations where flucytosine is unavailable (World Health Organization, 2018).
evidence: This statement describes the standard of care in Vietnam, supported by citation to WHO 2018 guidelines.

claim: Amphotericin combined with fluconazole is less effective than amphotericin with flucytosine, resulting in slower rates of fungal clearance and worse survival rates.
source: However, this combination is less effective than amphotericin with flucytosine, resulting in slower rates of fungal clearance and worse survival rates (Day et al., 2013; Molloy et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Day et al., 2013 and Molloy et al., 2018.

claim: The relationship between the rate of fungal clearance from CSF and survival is generally robust.
source: The relationship between the rate of fungal clearance from CSF and survival is generally robust; improving the potency of antifungal therapy is likely to be an effective way to reduce deaths (Day et al., 2013; Molloy et al., 2018; Beardsley et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Day et al., 2013, Molloy et al., 2018, and Beardsley et al., 2016.

claim: Improving the potency of antifungal therapy is likely to be an effective way to reduce deaths from cryptococcal meningitis.
source: The relationship between the rate of fungal clearance from CSF and survival is generally robust; improving the potency of antifungal therapy is likely to be an effective way to reduce deaths (Day et al., 2013; Molloy et al., 2018; Beardsley et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cited studies and represents a logical conclusion.

claim: Early fungicidal activity (EFA) is a sensitive measure able to detect differences between treatment regimens likely to be associated with survival benefits with far fewer patients than studies powered to survival itself.
source: The rate of clearance of yeast from CSF associated with an antifungal treatment (the early fungicidal activity, EFA) is a sensitive measure able to detect differences between treatment regimens likely to be associated with survival benefits with far fewer patients than studies powered to survival itself (Brouwer et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brouwer et al., 2004.

claim: Small studies powered to EFA endpoint can serve to filter treatment regimens that can be taken forward in larger trials.
source: Small studies powered to this endpoint can serve to filter treatment regimens that can be taken forward in larger trials (Brouwer et al., 2004; Bicanic et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brouwer et al., 2004 and Bicanic et al., 2009.

claim: The trial enrolled 50 patients in two hospitals in Ho Chi Minh City – the Hospital for Tropical Diseases and Cho Ray Hospital.
source: In brief, we enrolled 50 patients in two hospitals in Ho Chi Minh City – the Hospital for Tropical Diseases and Cho Ray Hospital.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the trial design and enrollment, supported by the trial data.

claim: Eligible adult patients were 18 years of age or older.
source: Eligible adult patients (≥18 years of age) had a clinical syndrome consistent with cryptococcal meningitis and one or more of: (1) positive cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) India ink; (2) C. neoformans cultured from CSF or blood; (3) positive cryptococcal antigen Lateral Flow Antigen Test (LFA) in CSF.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the trial inclusion criteria.

claim: All patients were tested for HIV infection in accordance with standard of care.
source: All patients were tested for HIV infection in accordance with standard of care.
evidence: This is a direct statement about trial procedures.

claim: Standard of care antifungal therapy consisted of intravenous amphotericin B deoxycholate 1 mg/kg/day combined with oral fluconazole 800 mg/day for the first 14 days following randomization.
source: Standard of care antifungal therapy consisted of intravenous amphotericin B deoxycholate 1 mg/kg/day (Amphotret, Bharat Serums and Vaccines, India) combined with oral fluconazole 800 mg/day (Zolmed, Glomed Pharmaceuticals, Vietnam) for the first 14 days following randomization.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the trial intervention protocol.

claim: Tamoxifen 300 mg/day was given orally in the intervention arm.
source: Tamoxifen (Nolvadex, AstraZeneca UK Ltd) 300 mg/day was given orally.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the trial intervention protocol.

claim: Randomization was in a ratio of 1:1, in blocks of 4 or 6, stratified by HIV serostatus and treating centre.
source: Randomization was in a ratio of 1:1, in blocks of 4 or 6, stratified by HIV serostatus (rapid test) and treating centre.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the trial randomization methodology.

claim: The primary outcome was Early Fungicidal Activity (EFA), defined as the rate of decline in culturable yeast from CSF over the first 2 weeks following randomization.
source: The primary outcome was Early Fungicidal Activity (EFA), defined as the rate of decline in culturable yeast from CSF over the first 2 weeks following randomization.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the trial's primary outcome measure.

claim: The study recruited between October 2017 and May 2018.
source: The study recruited between October 2017 and May 2018.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the trial timeline.

claim: 70 patients were screened for the trial.
source: We screened 70 patients, enrolling 50 (40 HIV infected; 10 HIV uninfected) with 24 assigned to the intervention arm and 26 assigned to the control arm.
evidence: This is directly stated in the results and shown in Figure 1.

claim: 40 HIV infected patients and 10 HIV uninfected patients were enrolled.
source: We screened 70 patients, enrolling 50 (40 HIV infected; 10 HIV uninfected) with 24 assigned to the intervention arm and 26 assigned to the control arm.
evidence: This is directly stated in the results section.

claim: 24 patients were assigned to the intervention arm and 26 to the control arm.
source: We screened 70 patients, enrolling 50 (40 HIV infected; 10 HIV uninfected) with 24 assigned to the intervention arm and 26 assigned to the control arm.
evidence: This is directly stated in the results section.

claim: One patient assigned to the intervention arm did not receive tamoxifen because of severe transaminitis.
source: One patient who was assigned to the intervention arm did not receive tamoxifen because of severe transaminitis.
evidence: This is directly stated in the results section.

claim: In the intention-to-treat analysis, the rates of fungal decline per day were −0.48 and −0.49 log10 colony-forming units (CFU)/ml/day in the control and tamoxifen groups respectively.
source: In the intention-to-treat analysis, the rates of fungal decline per day were −0.48 and −0.49 log10colony-forming units (CFU)/ml/day in the control and tamoxifen groups respectively (difference −0.005 log10 CFU/ml/day, 95% CI: −0.16, 0.15); p-value = 0.95, (see Table 2).
evidence: This is the primary outcome result directly stated and supported by data in Table 2.

claim: The difference in EFA between control and tamoxifen groups was −0.005 log10 CFU/ml/day (95% CI: −0.16, 0.15; p=0.95).
source: In the intention-to-treat analysis, the rates of fungal decline per day were −0.48 and −0.49 log10colony-forming units (CFU)/ml/day in the control and tamoxifen groups respectively (difference −0.005 log10 CFU/ml/day, 95% CI: −0.16, 0.15); p-value = 0.95, (see Table 2).
evidence: This is the primary outcome result directly stated and supported by data in Table 2.

claim: There was no detectable difference in EFA in the per-protocol population analysis.
source: There was no detectable difference in EFA in the per-protocol population analysis, or by HIV infection status (see Table 2).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data in Table 2.

claim: There was no detectable difference in EFA by HIV infection status.
source: There was no detectable difference in EFA in the per-protocol population analysis, or by HIV infection status (see Table 2).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data in Table 2.

claim: Death occurred in 8 of 24 patients in the tamoxifen group and 7 of 26 in the control group.
source: Death occured in 8 of 24 patients in the tamoxifen group and 7 of 26 in the control group (Kaplan-Meier mortality estimates 34% and 27% respectively, risk difference 6.5%; 95% confidence interval [CI], −19.2 to 32.1%; P=0.62 Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data in Table 3 and Figure 2B.

claim: Kaplan-Meier mortality estimates were 34% in the tamoxifen group and 27% in the control group.
source: Death occured in 8 of 24 patients in the tamoxifen group and 7 of 26 in the control group (Kaplan-Meier mortality estimates 34% and 27% respectively, risk difference 6.5%; 95% confidence interval [CI], −19.2 to 32.1%; P=0.62 Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data in Table 3 and Figure 2B.

claim: Fewer patients in the tamoxifen arm were classified as having a good outcome at 10 weeks compared with the control arm (9% versus 36%).
source: Fewer patients in the tamoxifen arm were classified as having a good outcome at 10 weeks compared with the control arm (9% versus 36%).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data in Table 3.

claim: There was no difference in change in CD4 counts in HIV patients by study arm over the 10-week period of follow-up.
source: We found no difference in change in CD4 counts in HIV patients by study arm over the 10-week period of follow-up (see Table 3).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data in Table 3.

claim: Eight patients had grade 3 or 4 QTc prolongation events in the tamoxifen arm, compared with one in the control arm (p=0.02).
source: Eight patients had grade 3 or 4 QTc prolongation events in the tamoxifen arm, compared with one in the control arm (p=0.02).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data in Table 4.

claim: Tamoxifen resulted in QTc prolongation over the 2-week treatment period (p<0.001).
source: Tamoxifen resulted in QTc prolongation over the 2-week treatment period (p<0.001).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Three patients in the tamoxifen arm had grade 3 or 4 ventricular extra-systole events compared with none in the control arm (p=0.21).
source: Three patients in the tamoxifen arm had grade 3 or 4 ventricular extra-systole events compared with none in the control arm (p=0.21).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data in Table 4.

claim: A 33-year-old male patient who had received tamoxifen suffered a cardiorespiratory arrest following a convulsion on day 21 of the study.
source: A 33-year-old male patient who had received tamoxifen suffered a cardiorespiratory arrest following a convulsion on day 21 of the study.
evidence: This is a direct report of an adverse event that occurred during the trial.

claim: All HIV infected patients had meningitis due to Cryptococcus neoformans molecular group VNI.
source: All HIV infected patients, and seven HIV uninfected patients, had meningitis due to Cryptococcus neoformans molecular group VNI.
evidence: This is directly stated based on microbiological testing performed in the trial.

claim: Seven HIV uninfected patients had meningitis due to Cryptococcus neoformans molecular group VNI.
source: All HIV infected patients, and seven HIV uninfected patients, had meningitis due to Cryptococcus neoformans molecular group VNI.
evidence: This is directly stated based on microbiological testing performed in the trial.

claim: Three HIV uninfected patients had disease due to Cryptococcus gattii (VGI).
source: Three HIV uninfected patients had disease due to Cryptococcus gattii (VGI).
evidence: This is directly stated based on microbiological testing performed in the trial.

claim: The MIC90 of amphotericin B was 2 mg/L.
source: The MIC90 of amphotericin B and fluconazole were 2 mg/L and 4 mg/L, respectively.
evidence: This is directly stated based on susceptibility testing performed in the trial.

claim: The MIC90 of fluconazole was 4 mg/L.
source: The MIC90 of amphotericin B and fluconazole were 2 mg/L and 4 mg/L, respectively.
evidence: This is directly stated based on susceptibility testing performed in the trial.

claim: The MIC90 of tamoxifen was 8 mg/L.
source: The MIC90 of tamoxifen was 8 mg/L.
evidence: This is directly stated based on susceptibility testing performed in the trial.

claim: Synergistic interaction (FICI ≤0.5) for tamoxifen combined with amphotericin was found in six isolates (12%).
source: This was ≤0.5 (suggestive of a possible synergistic interaction) for tamoxifen combined with amphotericin in six isolates (12%), and for tamoxifen combined with fluconazole in two isolates (4%).
evidence: This is directly stated based on FICI calculations from susceptibility testing in the trial.

claim: Synergistic interaction (FICI ≤0.5) for tamoxifen combined with fluconazole was found in two isolates (4%).
source: This was ≤0.5 (suggestive of a possible synergistic interaction) for tamoxifen combined with amphotericin in six isolates (12%), and for tamoxifen combined with fluconazole in two isolates (4%).
evidence: This is directly stated based on FICI calculations from susceptibility testing in the trial.

claim: The susceptibilities of the Cryptococcus isolates from this study to tamoxifen, fluconazole, and amphotericin were similar to those of isolates from previous clinical trials.
source: The susceptibilities of the Cryptococcus isolates from this study to tamoxifen, fluconazole, and amphotericin, were similar to those of isolates from our previous clinical trials (Hai et al., 2019; O'Connor et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hai et al., 2019 and O'Connor et al., 2020, comparing current data to historical data.

claim: Evidence of synergy when tamoxifen was combined with amphotericin was found in only 12% (95CI 5%, 24%) of isolates from the trial, compared with 67% (95CI 47%, 81%) in archived isolates.
source: However, in contrast with our previous findings we found evidence of synergy when tamoxifen was combined with amphotericin in only 12% (95CI 5%, 24%) of isolates from the trial. This compares with the rate in archived isolates of 67% (95CI 47%, 81%) (Hai et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim compares current trial data with previously published data cited from Hai et al., 2019.

claim: Synergy has been suggested as an explanation for the superiority of the amphotericin-flucytosine combination.
source: Synergy has been suggested as an explanation for the superiority of the amphotericin-flucytosine combination which has delivered improved yeast clearance and survival in a number of trials (Schwarz et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schwarz et al., 2003.

claim: Tamoxifen is concentrated in the brain 10- to 100-fold and in macrophage phagosomes.
source: Given that tamoxifen is concentrated in the brain (10- to 100-fold), and in macrophage phagosomes, we consider it unlikely that we did not reach drug concentrations greater than the MIC90 at the disease site, although it is possible that absorption of orally administered drug was impaired in our patients.
evidence: This statement draws on previously cited knowledge about tamoxifen pharmacokinetics and represents an inference about drug concentrations in the trial.

claim: It is possible that absorption of orally administered tamoxifen was impaired in the trial patients.
source: Given that tamoxifen is concentrated in the brain (10- to 100-fold), and in macrophage phagosomes, we consider it unlikely that we did not reach drug concentrations greater than the MIC90 at the disease site, although it is possible that absorption of orally administered drug was impaired in our patients.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible explanation for the trial results.

claim: There was greater prolongation of the QTc interval in patients on tamoxifen.
source: However, there was greater prolongation of the QTc interval in patients on tamoxifen.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 3 and Table 4.

claim: The mechanism through which tamoxifen causes QT interval prolongation in humans is unknown.
source: The mechanism through which tamoxifen causes QT interval prolongation in humans is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge regarding tamoxifen's mechanism of action.

claim: In animals there is evidence that tamoxifen's QT prolongation is due to multi-channel block, inhibiting both IKR and ICa channels.
source: In animals there is evidence that the block is multi-channel, due to both inhibition of the IKR and ICa channels (Asp et al., 2013; He et al., 2003; Liu et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Asp et al., 2013, He et al., 2003, and Liu et al., 1998.

claim: Multi-channel block is considered to confer a reduced risk of life-threatening arrhythmias compared with drugs that block single ion channels.
source: Such multi-channel block is considered to confer a reduced risk of life-threatening arrhythmias compared with drugs that block single ion channels.
evidence: This statement reflects established pharmacological knowledge about cardiac ion channel effects.

claim: There were no cases of ventricular tachycardia in the study.
source: While we did not have any cases of ventricular tachycardia in our study, there was an episode of cardiac arrest in the tamoxifen arm.
evidence: This is directly stated based on adverse event monitoring in the trial.

claim: There was an episode of cardiac arrest in the tamoxifen arm.
source: While we did not have any cases of ventricular tachycardia in our study, there was an episode of cardiac arrest in the tamoxifen arm.
evidence: This is directly stated based on adverse event monitoring in the trial.

claim: The cardiac arrest occurred on day 21, 1 week after administration of tamoxifen had finished.
source: The cardiac arrest in our study occurred on day 21, 1 week after administration of tamoxifen had finished.
evidence: This is directly stated based on the timing of the adverse event.

claim: Tamoxifen has a half-life of 5 to 7 days.
source: However, given tamoxifen's half-life of 5 to 7 days, and the doses used, it is possible that this event was related.
evidence: This is a statement of established pharmacokinetic knowledge about tamoxifen.

claim: It is possible that the cardiac arrest was related to tamoxifen.
source: However, given tamoxifen's half-life of 5 to 7 days, and the doses used, it is possible that this event was related.
evidence: This is speculation about the possible relationship between tamoxifen and the adverse event.

claim: Fluconazole is a recognised cause of QT prolongation.
source: Fluconazole is also a recognised cause of QT prolongation.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about fluconazole's adverse effects.

claim: Fluconazole's QT prolongation mechanism is believed to be through modulation of the Ikr current of the cardiac depolarization cycle.
source: Here, the mechanism is believed to be through modulation of the Ikr current of the cardiac depolarization cycle (Han et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Han et al., 2011.

claim: There was little evidence of significant QT prolongation in patients in the control arm of the study.
source: However, we found little evidence of significant QT prolongation in patients in the control arm of our study, and in fact the acute effect of administration of fluconazole was shortening of the QTc interval.
evidence: This is directly stated based on QTc monitoring data from the trial.

claim: The acute effect of administration of fluconazole was shortening of the QTc interval.
source: However, we found little evidence of significant QT prolongation in patients in the control arm of our study, and in fact the acute effect of administration of fluconazole was shortening of the QTc interval.
evidence: This is directly stated based on QTc monitoring data from the trial.

claim: Sertraline has in vitro fungicidal activity against Cryptococcus neoformans and a synergistic effect when combined with fluconazole.
source: Sertraline has in vitro fungicidal activity against Cryptococcus neoformans and a synergistic effect when combined with fluconazole.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge from prior research on sertraline.

claim: Results from a pilot dose-finding study of adjunctive sertraline for cryptococcal meningitis suggested it was a safe and potentially effective treatment.
source: Results from a pilot dose-finding study of adjunctive sertraline for cryptococcal meningitis suggested it was a safe and potentially effective treatment, although no contemporaneous controls were enrolled in the trial (Rhein et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rhein et al., 2016.

claim: A large randomized controlled trial of sertraline powered to mortality was stopped due to futility having enrolled 460 patients.
source: Subsequently a large randomized controlled trial powered to mortality was stopped due to futility having enrolled 460 patients (Rhein et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rhein et al., 2019.

claim: There was no difference in survival or EFA between the standard therapy or sertraline boosted treatment arms in the large sertraline trial.
